implementation_notes: pytest is the dominant Python test framework and its plugin ecosystem supplies the record/compare/approve loop: syrupy adds a snapshot fixture whose equality assertion compares the value against a committed reference in __snapshots__/ and creates or updates it when the suite runs with --snapshot-update; pytest-snapshot offers the same idea with a different API. pytest core contributes the rest of the harness - capsys/capfd capture stdout and stderr at sys or file-descriptor level, tmp_path gives per-test scratch space, and parametrize feeds the input corpus. Prefer this variant when the team already accepts a test-only plugin, and treat re-recording as a reviewed act.
pitfalls: Reference files live next to the tests in __snapshots__/ and are updated in bulk by --snapshot-update; re-record one test at a time so the approval stays a review.
capsys only captures Python-level writes: output produced by C extensions or subprocesses needs capfd (file-descriptor level) or the captured subprocess output, or the golden records nothing.
The snapshot format is versioned by the plugin; upgrading across majors can rewrite every reference and must be a deliberate, reviewed change.

variants.name: Hand-written golden files with a pytest --update option
variants.idiom_name: pytest fixture over files under tests/golden/, rewritten only with --update
variants.implementation_notes: A twenty-line fixture does the same job without a plugin: read the reference file, compare, and rewrite it only when the session was started with --update (registered through pytest_addoption), so the artefact format, directory layout and diff output are entirely yours. Choose it when references must be plain data files consumed by other tools, when the plugin's own file format is unwelcome, or when you want the update path visible in the suite's own code.
pitfalls: Registering --update in a plugin forces the flag onto every run; keep it opt-in and make the CI invocation explicit so a pipeline never rewrites references.
A missing golden must fail the test; a helper that writes on absence turns the first run into an accidental recording of the current (possibly buggy) build.
